sections.skill: Verify surprising media by checking source and context

questions.domain: Creative: audio, music, video and synthetic media
questions.prompt: What is a deepfake?

choices.text: Any video that has been edited at all, including trimming silence
Realistic fake media showing someone doing what they did not

questions.correct_answer: Realistic fake media showing someone doing what they did not
questions.intro: A DEEPFAKE is realistic generated or altered media that shows someone saying or doing something they did not. Spotting one by a single visual oddity, such as strange blinking or blurry ears, is unreliable: real videos have glitches too, and newer fakes may have none. Better checks look at SOURCE and CONTEXT. Who first posted it? Do trusted news outlets or the person's official accounts report it? Does a reverse image search find older, original versions? Does it fit known facts about time and place? A surprising clip that makes you angry or scared deserves the most checking.

sections.skill: Verify a clip with four questions

questions.domain: Creative: audio, music, video and synthetic media
questions.prompt: A clip posted by a brand-new anonymous account fails which question?
questions.correct_answer: Source
questions.intro: Before believing or sharing a surprising clip, ask four questions. (1) SOURCE: who posted it first, and are they trustworthy? (2) CONFIRMATION: do trusted outlets or the person's official accounts report it? (3) EARLIER VERSIONS: does a reverse image search find an original that is different? (4) CONTEXT: do the date, place and weather fit? Example: a "live" video of snow in a desert city on a day that was 35 °C, posted by a brand-new account, fails questions 1 and 4.

sections.skill: Avoid both mistakes and respond to harmful fakes

questions.domain: Creative: audio, music, video and synthetic media
questions.prompt: What are the two common mistakes?

choices.text: Believing fakes and dismissing real evidence as AI
Using reverse search and reading captions
Checking sources too carefully and asking trusted news outlets whether events really happened

questions.correct_answer: Believing fakes and dismissing real evidence as AI
questions.intro: Two mistakes are common. One is believing a fake because it looks real. The other is dismissing real evidence as "probably AI," which lets people deny things they really did. Both are avoided by checking sources rather than trusting looks. Some deepfakes cause serious harm, such as nonconsensual intimate images. In the United States, the TAKE IT DOWN Act requires covered platforms, from May 19, 2026, to offer a removal process and act on valid requests within 48 hours. Report such content, and do not share it.
